voiceover: In the late 1800s, observers described it as wide enough to hold about three Earths side by side.
visual: Scale diagram: three Earths inside a large oval

voiceover: As of the mid-2020s, it's only about 1.3 times Earth's width, and it has become rounder.
visual: Scale diagram: smaller oval with one Earth inside

voiceover: Its winds still blow at hundreds of kilometers per hour, much faster than the strongest hurricanes on Earth.
visual: Animated icons: swirling arrows with a speed label

voiceover: Nobody knows exactly why it's shrinking. Scientists are still studying how it feeds on smaller storms.
visual: Animated icons: small storms merging into a big one

voiceover: So any size you quote for it needs a date attached. Check before you post, every time.
visual: Calendar icon next to a ruler icon

voiceover: Do you think the Great Red Spot will ever vanish? Comment below.
visual: Storm icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Space wouldn't make you explode.
visual: Stock clip of a starfield with a suit icon

voiceover: Without a suit in vacuum, you wouldn't burst or freeze solid in an instant.
visual: Animated icons: burst and ice icons crossed out

voiceover: The real danger is oxygen. With no air pressure, your lungs empty and your blood quickly runs low on oxygen.
visual: Simple diagram: lungs with outward arrows, O2 meter falling

voiceover: Studies of accidents in vacuum chambers suggest you'd stay conscious for only about 10 to 15 seconds.
visual: Big number card: 10–15 seconds

voiceover: Your skin and tissues would swell, but your skin is strong enough to hold you together. Your blood stays inside you.
visual: Simple diagram: body outline swelling slightly

voiceover: Saliva on your tongue could start to bubble, because liquids boil at very low pressure even when they aren't hot.
visual: Animated icons: water drop with bubbles, pressure gauge at zero

voiceover: Animal studies and rare accidents suggest a quick rescue, within about a minute, may be survivable.
visual: Animated icons: clock at 60 s, rescue arrow

voiceover: Which space myth did movies teach you? Comment below.
visual: Myth icon + comment bubble

voiceover: The Sun has an eleven-year mood cycle.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of the Sun with sunspots

voiceover: Every eleven years or so, it swings from quiet to stormy and back. It's called the solar cycle.
visual: Simple chart: wave line with peaks about 11 years apart

voiceover: At its peak, more dark sunspots appear. They're cooler patches where tangled magnetic fields hold back the heat.
visual: Simple diagram: sunspot with tangled field lines

voiceover: Some sunspots are wider than Earth, yet they only look dark next to the brighter surface around them.
visual: Scale diagram: Earth beside a sunspot

voiceover: More sunspots also mean more solar flares and huge clouds of charged particles thrown out into space.
visual: Animated icons: flare burst, particle cloud leaving the Sun

voiceover: When those clouds reach Earth, they can trigger bright auroras far from the poles and disturb satellites and radio signals.
visual: Stock clip of an aurora over a landscape

voiceover: Then the Sun calms down again, and for a while sunspots can almost disappear. The magnetic field also flips each cycle.
visual: Animated icons: spots fading, magnet icon flipping

voiceover: Have you ever seen an aurora? Tell me where.
visual: Aurora icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Saturn has so many moons, the count keeps changing.
visual: Saturn icon beside a fast-spinning number counter

voiceover: At last count, Saturn has well over two hundred confirmed moons. That's more than any other planet we know.
visual: Public-domain agency image of Saturn, credit shown

voiceover: Most of them are tiny. Many are just a few kilometers across, more like captured rocks than round worlds.
visual: Scale diagram: tiny moon next to a city outline

voiceover: Astronomers find them by stacking many telescope images until faint dots moving with Saturn stand out.
visual: Animated icons: stacked frames, one dot circled

voiceover: But a few are giants. Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury and has a thick, hazy atmosphere.
visual: Scale diagram: Titan beside Mercury, both labelled

voiceover: And little Enceladus sprays jets of water ice into space from cracks near its south pole.
visual: Artist's impression of Enceladus jets, labelled

voiceover: So the next time someone quotes a moon count, check the date. The number keeps climbing.
visual: Counter icon next to a calendar icon

voiceover: Which moon would you visit first, Titan or Enceladus? Tell me below.
visual: Titan and Enceladus icons + comment bubble

voiceover: In 1967, a strange signal ticked like a clock.
visual: Animated icons: radio dish with pulse marks

voiceover: A radio telescope picked up pulses arriving about every 1.3 seconds, steady and precise.
visual: Simple chart: evenly spaced pulse spikes

voiceover: The team half-jokingly nicknamed it LGM-1, for little green men, because nothing natural seemed that regular.
visual: Simple graphic: LGM-1 label with a wink icon

voiceover: It turned out to be a pulsar: a spinning neutron star, the crushed core of an exploded star.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of a pulsar with two beams

voiceover: Pulsars shoot beams of radio waves from their magnetic poles. As they spin, the beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.
visual: Animated diagram: rotating beams sweeping past Earth

voiceover: Some spin hundreds of times every second, and their ticks are so regular they can rival atomic clocks.
visual: Animated icons: fast spinning dot beside a clock

voiceover: Scientists now use networks of pulsars to search for faint ripples in space itself, called gravitational waves.
visual: Simple diagram: several pulsars linked to Earth by lines

voiceover: Would you have guessed aliens too? Be honest below.
visual: Pulsar icon + comment bubble

voiceover: We've found thousands of planets around other stars.
visual: Stock clip of a star field, dots lighting up

voiceover: As of the mid-2020s, the confirmed count is more than 5,000, and it keeps climbing.
visual: Counter icon climbing past 5,000

voiceover: Just over thirty years ago, we didn't know of a single planet around a Sun-like star.
visual: Simple timeline: empty bar, then rising line

voiceover: Most are found by watching a star dim slightly when a planet passes in front of it, like a tiny eclipse.
visual: Simple chart: light curve with a small dip

voiceover: Others show up as a wobble, as the planet's gravity tugs its star back and forth.
visual: Animated diagram: star wobbling as a planet orbits

voiceover: Many are nothing like our planets: giant worlds hugging their stars, or planets between Earth and Neptune in size.
visual: Scale diagram: Earth, mid-size planet, Neptune

voiceover: Because so many stars seem to have planets, there may be more planets than stars in our galaxy.
visual: Animated icons: stars each gaining small planet dots

voiceover: Which kind of alien world would you visit first? Tell me below.
visual: Planet icons + comment bubble

voiceover: A spacecraft ended its mission by diving into Saturn.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of a probe above Saturn

voiceover: Cassini reached Saturn in 2004 and spent about thirteen years studying the planet, its rings and moons.
visual: Simple timeline: 2004 to 2017

voiceover: It carried the Huygens probe to Titan, and found water jets on Enceladus hinting at a hidden ocean.
visual: Animated icons: probe dropping to a moon, icy jets

voiceover: By 2017, it was running out of fuel. Left alone, it might one day have crashed into one of those moons.
visual: Animated icons: fuel gauge near empty

voiceover: Mission teams didn't want any Earth microbes on board to reach a moon that might support life.
visual: Simple graphic: microbe icon with a stop sign

voiceover: So they flew it through the gap between Saturn and its rings 22 times, gathering data no probe had collected before.
visual: Animated diagram: orbit loops threading the ring gap

voiceover: In September 2017, Cassini plunged into Saturn's atmosphere, sending data until it broke apart.
visual: Animated icons: probe streak entering a planet's clouds

voiceover: Was that a fitting ending for Cassini? Tell me what you think.
visual: Probe icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Space is closer than you think.
visual: Stock clip of clouds from high altitude

voiceover: Space is often said to begin about 100 kilometers up, roughly an hour's drive straight up.
visual: Simple diagram: car on a vertical road, 100 km mark

voiceover: That line is a convention, not a wall. Some agencies use about 80 kilometers instead, so definitions differ.
visual: Simple diagram: two dashed lines at 80 and 100 km

voiceover: The hard part isn't height. To stay in orbit, you need to fly sideways at about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
visual: Animated diagram: object circling Earth, speed label

voiceover: That's why only a small group of people have ever gone. As of the mid-2020s, it's more than 600 people.
visual: Counter icon passing 600

voiceover: The count depends on which boundary you use, and it grows with every crewed flight.
visual: Simple graphic: two counters side by side

voiceover: Compared with more than eight billion people on Earth, that's a tiny club. Most of them flew to orbit, not just above the line.
visual: Scale diagram: tiny dot cluster beside a huge crowd

voiceover: If you got a free seat, would you take it? Comment below.
visual: Seat icon + comment bubble

voiceover: You can't see the Great Wall from the Moon.
visual: Stock clip of the Great Wall from the ground

voiceover: It's one of the most repeated space myths, and it was in print long before anyone flew to space.
visual: Simple graphic: old book icon with a myth stamp

voiceover: The wall is very long, but in most places it's only a few meters wide, about as wide as a road.
visual: Scale diagram: wall width next to a road

voiceover: From the Moon, about 384,000 kilometers away, even whole continents look small. A road-width line is far too thin to see.
visual: Public-domain agency image of Earth from far away, credit shown

voiceover: Even from the space station, about 400 kilometers up, astronauts say it's extremely hard to spot without help.
visual: Simple diagram: station orbit 400 km above Earth

voiceover: Its color blends in with the land around it, which makes it harder to pick out than its length suggests.
visual: Simple graphic: grey line fading into brown terrain

voiceover: Meanwhile, city lights at night, big airports and highways can stand out clearly from orbit.
visual: Public-domain agency image of city lights at night, credit shown

voiceover: Where did you first hear the Great Wall myth? Comment below.
visual: Wall icon + comment bubble

voiceover: The closest planet to the Sun isn't the hottest.
visual: Simple diagram: Sun, Mercury and Venus in a row

voiceover: Mercury sits closest, yet Venus is hotter, at around 465 degrees Celsius, day and night.
visual: Animated icons: two thermometers, Venus higher

voiceover: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so heat escapes easily. Its day side can reach about 430 degrees Celsius.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of Mercury's cratered surface

voiceover: But its night side drops to about minus 180 degrees, one of the biggest temperature swings in the solar system.
visual: Simple chart: temperature bar from 430 to minus 180

voiceover: Venus is the opposite. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat like a greenhouse with the windows shut.
visual: Simple diagram: heat arrows trapped under a thick layer

voiceover: That's hot enough to melt lead, and it barely cools at night, because the heat has nowhere to go.
visual: Animated icons: lead block melting

voiceover: Even stranger, scientists have found evidence of water ice in shadowed craters near Mercury's poles.
visual: Simple diagram: polar crater in shadow with ice label

voiceover: Which would you rather survive for one minute, Mercury or Venus? Tell me below.
visual: Planet icons + comment bubble

voiceover: Jupiter's moon Io is covered in erupting volcanoes.
visual: Public-domain agency image of Io, credit shown

voiceover: It's thought to be the most volcanically active world we know of, with hundreds of active volcanoes.
visual: Simple graphic: Io disk with many volcano dots

voiceover: Some lava lakes are larger than cities, and some plumes shoot material hundreds of kilometers above the surface.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of a tall volcanic plume

voiceover: Io is about the size of our Moon, so where does all that heat come from? Not from the Sun.
visual: Scale diagram: Io beside our Moon

voiceover: Jupiter's huge gravity, plus tugs from neighboring moons, keeps squeezing Io as it moves along its slightly stretched orbit.
visual: Animated diagram: oval orbit, Io squeezed near Jupiter

voiceover: Its solid surface rises and falls by up to about 100 meters, and that flexing heats the inside like a squeezed stress ball.
visual: Animated icons: stress ball squeezed, heat lines

voiceover: The result is a yellow, orange and black world painted by sulfur, constantly resurfaced by fresh lava.
visual: Simple graphic: yellow, orange and black color swatches

voiceover: Would you risk a flyby of Io for the view? Tell me below.
visual: Io icon + comment bubble

voiceover: The Sun's outer atmosphere is hotter than its surface.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of the Sun's corona

voiceover: The visible surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius. That's already hot enough to melt any metal we know.
visual: Big number card: about 5,500 °C

voiceover: But the corona, the thin glowing atmosphere above it, reaches more than a million degrees.
visual: Big number card: 1,000,000+ °C

voiceover: That's like walking away from a campfire and feeling the air get hotter. It shouldn't work that way.
visual: Animated icons: campfire, thermometer rising with distance

voiceover: This is called the coronal heating problem, and scientists have been working on it for decades.
visual: Simple graphic: puzzle piece over the Sun

voiceover: Leading ideas involve magnetic fields: waves carrying energy upward, and countless small explosions where magnetic lines snap and reconnect.
visual: Simple diagram: magnetic loops snapping with tiny flashes

voiceover: As of the mid-2020s, spacecraft flying close to the Sun are still testing these ideas.
visual: Animated icons: generic probe near a glowing Sun

voiceover: Which space mystery should I cover next? Tell me below.
visual: Question mark icon + comment bubble

voiceover: A giant black hole sits at our galaxy's center.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of a galactic center

voiceover: It's called Sagittarius A star, and it has about four million times the mass of the Sun.
visual: Big number card: about 4,000,000 Suns

voiceover: Don't worry, it's about 26,000 light-years away, and Earth is in no danger from it.
visual: Scale diagram: Sun's position far from the center

voiceover: Astronomers found it by tracking stars near the galactic center for decades, watching them whip around an invisible object.
visual: Animated diagram: star orbits around an empty point

voiceover: One star swings so close that it reaches thousands of kilometers per second at its nearest point.
visual: Animated icons: star speeding up near the center

voiceover: Only something incredibly massive and compact could pull those orbits so tight, and a black hole fits the evidence.
visual: Simple diagram: tight ellipses around a dark dot

voiceover: In 2022, astronomers released the first image of its shadow, a glowing ring much like the one seen in galaxy M87.
visual: Simple graphic: two glowing rings side by side

voiceover: Did you know our galaxy has a black hole at its heart? Comment below.
visual: Galaxy icon + comment bubble

voiceover: The universe's oldest light is all around you.
visual: Stock clip of a night sky slowly brightening

voiceover: It's called the cosmic microwave background, a faint glow that fills the whole sky in every direction.
visual: Simple graphic: whole-sky oval map with mottled colors

voiceover: It was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled enough for light to travel freely.
visual: Simple timeline: Big Bang to 380,000 years

voiceover: That light has traveled for nearly 14 billion years, and expanding space has stretched it into faint microwaves.
visual: Animated icons: wave line stretching longer

voiceover: It was first detected in 1965 by two radio astronomers who thought the hiss in their antenna might be pigeon droppings.
visual: Simple graphic: horn antenna icon with a bird icon

voiceover: You've probably heard that old TV static includes it. A small part of that static did come from this ancient glow.
visual: Stock clip of analog TV static

voiceover: Maps of its tiny temperature differences show the seeds that later grew into galaxies, including ours.
visual: Simple graphic: mottled map zooming into galaxy icons

voiceover: Does it amaze you that old static held Big Bang light? Comment below.
visual: TV icon + comment bubble

voiceover: People have lived in orbit nonstop since 2000.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of a space station over Earth

voiceover: The International Space Station has had a crew on board continuously since November 2000.
visual: Simple timeline starting at November 2000

voiceover: As of the mid-2020s, that's more than two decades without a single day empty.
visual: Counter icon showing years, still running

voiceover: It orbits about 400 kilometers up and circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes, so the crew sees about 16 sunrises a day.
visual: Animated diagram: orbit loop with a 90-minute timer

voiceover: It's about the size of a football field, built piece by piece in orbit by several space agencies working together.
visual: Scale diagram: station outline over a football field

voiceover: On a clear night, you can see it without a telescope: a bright, steady dot gliding across the sky in a few minutes.
visual: Stock clip of night sky, moving dot graphic

voiceover: It won't last forever. Its partners have announced plans to retire it in the coming years.
visual: Simple timeline with a fading end

voiceover: Have you ever spotted the station? Tell me where you saw it.
visual: Station icon + comment bubble

voiceover: The longest single spaceflight lasted about 437 days.
visual: Big number card: about 437 days

voiceover: As of the mid-2020s, that record still belongs to Valeri Polyakov, a Russian doctor and cosmonaut.
visual: Simple graphic: record badge with a calendar

voiceover: He flew to the Mir space station in 1994 and came home in 1995, after more than fourteen months in orbit.
visual: Simple timeline: 1994 to 1995

voiceover: As a doctor, part of his mission was to study what a long stay does to the human body and mind.
visual: Animated icons: stethoscope, brain and heart icons

voiceover: That question matters for Mars. A round trip there could take well over a year, even with a short stay.
visual: Simple diagram: Earth to Mars path with a calendar

voiceover: After landing, he chose to walk a short distance from the capsule instead of being carried.
visual: Animated icons: footsteps leaving a capsule outline

voiceover: Long stays still cause bone loss, muscle loss and eye changes, so researchers keep studying crews on long missions.
visual: Simple graphic: three health icons with arrows

voiceover: Could you spend fourteen months in a small space station? Comment below.
visual: Calendar icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Stars twinkle. Planets mostly shine steadily.
visual: Stock clip of a twinkling night sky

voiceover: The stars themselves aren't flickering. The twinkle happens in Earth's air, not in space.
visual: Simple diagram: star, atmosphere layer, eye

voiceover: Our atmosphere is full of moving pockets of warmer and cooler air that bend light slightly as it passes through.
visual: Animated icons: wavy air layers bending a light ray

voiceover: A star is so far away that it's basically a single point of light, so every tiny bend makes it jump and flicker.
visual: Simple graphic: single dot jittering

voiceover: Planets are much closer, so they appear as tiny disks. The flickers from different parts of the disk average out.
visual: Simple diagram: small disk made of many points

voiceover: That's a handy trick: if a bright dot shines steadily, there's a good chance it's a planet.
visual: Simple graphic: steady dot labelled planet

voiceover: Stars near the horizon twinkle most, because their light crosses more air. Astronauts above the air see steady stars.
visual: Simple diagram: long low light path vs short high path

voiceover: Have you used the twinkle test to find a planet? Tell me below.
visual: Star icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Neptune was predicted with math before it was spotted.
visual: Animated icons: equation lines turning into a blue planet

voiceover: In the 1800s, astronomers noticed Uranus wasn't moving quite where its orbit said it should be.
visual: Simple diagram: predicted path vs actual path of Uranus

voiceover: Something unseen seemed to be tugging on it. A French mathematician, Urbain Le Verrier, worked out where that something must be.
visual: Animated icons: invisible tug arrow, pencil and paper

voiceover: In 1846, he sent his prediction to the Berlin Observatory, and astronomers there found the planet the very first night they looked.
visual: Simple sky chart with an X marking the spot

voiceover: It was within about one degree of the predicted spot, a tiny patch of sky.
visual: Simple graphic: small circle around the X

voiceover: An English mathematician, John Couch Adams, had made similar calculations, and both are now often credited.
visual: Simple graphic: two pencil icons side by side

voiceover: Neptune is so far out that one year there lasts about 165 Earth years. It finished its first full orbit since discovery in 2011.
visual: Animated diagram: one full orbit loop, 1846 to 2011

voiceover: Would you rather find a planet with math or a telescope? Comment below.
visual: Math and telescope icons + comment bubble

voiceover: Our Moon may have formed from a giant collision.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of two young worlds colliding

voiceover: The leading idea is that a Mars-sized body slammed into the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
visual: Scale diagram: young Earth and a Mars-sized body

voiceover: Scientists often call that body Theia. The impact would have blasted molten rock and vapor into orbit around Earth.
visual: Animated icons: debris ring forming around Earth

voiceover: Over time, that debris clumped together and formed the Moon, possibly much closer to Earth than it is today.
visual: Animated diagram: ring clumping into a Moon

voiceover: Evidence: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo crews are strikingly similar to Earth's rocks in their chemistry.
visual: Simple graphic: two rock icons with matching labels

voiceover: The Moon also has a small iron core, which fits the idea that it formed mostly from rocky outer layers.
visual: Simple diagram: Moon cut-away with a small core

voiceover: Some details are still debated, like how much of the Moon came from Theia, but the collision idea leads the field.
visual: Simple graphic: question mark beside a leading badge

voiceover: Does a collision origin make the Moon more fascinating to you? Comment below.
visual: Moon icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Auroras happen at both ends of the Earth.
visual: Stock clip of a green aurora

voiceover: Many people know the northern lights, but the southern lights are just as real, around the Antarctic region.
visual: Simple globe graphic: rings at both poles

voiceover: They start with the Sun, which constantly sends out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind.
visual: Animated icons: particles streaming from the Sun

voiceover: Earth's magnetic field steers many of those particles toward the polar regions, where they slam into our upper atmosphere.
visual: Simple diagram: field lines guiding particles to the poles

voiceover: When they hit oxygen and nitrogen, those gases glow. Oxygen often gives green, and sometimes red at higher altitudes.
visual: Simple graphic: color key, green and red labelled oxygen

voiceover: Nitrogen can add blue and purple tints, which is why the edges of some displays look violet.
visual: Simple graphic: blue and purple swatches labelled nitrogen

voiceover: During big solar storms, auroras can reach much farther from the poles, and phone cameras often catch colors our eyes miss.
visual: Animated icons: phone camera showing brighter colors

voiceover: Northern or southern lights: which would you travel to see? Comment below.
visual: Aurora icons + comment bubble
